A political newsletter for normal people.
WTF Just Happened Today? is a sane, once-a-day newsletter helping normal people make sense of the news. Curated daily and delivered to 200,000+ people every afternoon around 3 pm Pacific.
Day 2051: “A regretful response.”
Today in One Sentence. A Postal Service whistleblower warned that the agency’s new mail-voting system could lead to a “catastrophic failure” ahead of the midterms; the House passed a stopgap funding bill to keep the government open through Dec. 11; the U.S. launched “large and powerful” strikes on Iranian targets; Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned following months of disagreements with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth; and the CDC excluded Pennsylvania’s two measles-associated deaths from its national count.
1/ A Postal Service whistleblower warned that the agency’s new mail-voting system could lead to a “catastrophic failure” ahead of the midterms. The anonymous federal official described the effort to carry out Trump’s restrictions on mail voting as “secretive, rushed” and “risky and haphazard.” The whistleblower alleged that USPS gave itself roughly three months to build a system that would normally take nine months to a year, and warned that the portal was “untested” and would have “significant operating problems” when released. The Postal Service also adopted a “zero-percent failure policy,” under which one barcode that fails to scan or match the submitted information could cause an entire batch – potentially thousands or tens of thousands of ballots – to be rejected until the discrepancy is resolved. The disclosure called the process “entirely unforgiving” and warned that “potentially millions of American voters” may not receive their mail-in ballots in time or at all. While a federal judge has blocked the mandatory implementation of the system for now, they allowed USPS to continue building it so long as states aren’t required to use it. (Associated Press / New York Times / Axios / Washington Post / NBC News / CNN / NPR / CBS News / The Guardian)
- The Commerce Department removed explicit bans on political interference from its scientific integrity policy. The Aug. 19 revision deleted language banning officials from suppressing, delaying, or altering scientific findings for political purposes. It applies to the Census Bureau, NOAA, and the Bureau of Economic Analysis. (NPR)
2/ The House passed a stopgap funding bill to keep the government open through Dec. 11, punting negotiations over the full-year funding plan until after the midterm elections. The measure keeps spending largely at current levels, blocks the Trump administration from transferring new funds to Border Patrol, and temporarily prevents political appointees from canceling federal grants. The Senate approved it last month, and Trump is expected to sign it. (Reuters / NPR / New York Times / Wall Street Journal / The Guardian / Axios / CBS News / NBC News)
- Trump urged Congress to immediately pass a federal film and television tax incentive. He didn’t propose a specific credit, but the industry has floated incentives of roughly 15% to 20%. (Reuters / Wall Street Journal / Washington Post / The Hill / NBC News)
3/ The U.S. launched “large and powerful” strikes on Iranian targets. Trump said the strikes were in “retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait,” and for an earlier attack on a military base in Jordan. Trump warned that if the Islamic Republic retaliates, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings.” He added that “there will be very little left” of the country. Hours later, however, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced that the country had launched a “regretful response.” (New York Times / Politico / Bloomberg / Wall Street Journal / CNBC / CNN / The Guardian / NBC News)
4/ Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned following months of disagreements with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Driscoll told Trump he was frustrated that Hegseth had fired generals involved in the Army’s transformation efforts and blocked promotions of senior Army officers. His departure leaves the Army without Senate-confirmed civilian or military leadership after Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George in April. (Wall Street Journal / Politico / NBC News / Reuters / New York Times / Bloomberg / Axios / Washington Post / CNN)
- Former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino was under internal investigation for alleged misconduct when he retired from Customs and Border Protection in March. CBP notified Bovino on March 2 that it had opened an official inquiry into alleged misconduct. 16 days later, he submitted a retirement relocation request. Bovino claimed the investigations were weaponized to force him out, while CBP said he “voluntarily retired.” (CBS News / The Hill / Chicago Tribune)
5/ The CDC excluded Pennsylvania’s two measles-associated deaths from its national count. Despite Pennsylvania providing the CDC with the required epidemiological data and that both unvaccinated residents tested positive for measles, the agency said the “available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths.” Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., meanwhile, suggested without evidence that the deaths may have been “fabricated.” (Washington Post / Philadelphia Inquirer / The Guardian / New York Times)
The 2026 midterms are in 63 days; the 2028 presidential election is in 798 days.

sources.text:
Postal Service whistleblower predicts ‘catastrophic’ effects from Trump mail voting order
A U.S. Postal Service whistleblower in a report published Sept. 1, 2026, alleged that USPS rushed the development of electronic tools to comply with a Trump administration policy placing new restrictions on mail-in voting. (Photo by Simone Hogan/Getty Images)
The U.S. Postal Service rushed the development of electronic tools to comply with a Trump administration policy placing new restrictions on mail-in voting, and defied a court order to stop work on the system, according to an explosive whistleblower complaint published Tuesday by Democratic U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal.
The unnamed whistleblower predicted the result could be “foreseeable catastrophic disruption to our coming nationwide elections based on the reckless pursuit of readying a new, insufficiently tested, poorly planned mail-in ballot screening system.”
The system contains several massive flaws and, with virtually no time to spare before the November elections, USPS officials kept on developing an online verification system in violation of a Massachusetts judge’s injunction, the whistleblower said.
The system’s verification standard is “a zero percent failure rate,” meaning that any batch of ballots that contain any single ballot with an error would result in an entire batch being rejected, the whistleblower said.
The verification system itself is suspect due to a hurried and untested development of an online portal that states were to use to upload voter and ballot information for verification by federal officials, the whistleblower said.
Up against a tight timeline ahead of the midterm elections, the agency also continued to develop an online tool related to the regulation, despite the federal court order to pause the work, according to the whistleblower.
No specific USPS officials were named as responsible for directing the work to continue in defiance of the courts. USPS did not immediately return a request for comment from States Newsroom.
States were expected to begin using the system as soon as Tuesday, according to the whistleblower.
Potential for millions of missing ballots
The allegations from the whistleblower, a federal official whose exact role is not specified, were detailed in a report by Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit legal group that is representing the whistleblower.
Blumenthal, of Connecticut, attached the report to a letter to U.S. Postmaster General David Steiner.
“The apparently sloppy and rushed manner in which the Federal Ballot Mail Portal and supporting IT systems are being built poses significant risk,” the report said. “Potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all.”
The new policy, which President Donald Trump initiated in a March executive order, has been the subject of intense legal fighting over the past few weeks that continues with an appeal now sitting at the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals. Democratic state officials and voting rights groups have said the regulation would likely disenfranchise voters.
Blumenthal said the USPS should reject the policy entirely.
“We urge you to abandon this ill-conceived, unconscionable plan and ensure that all Americans can exercise their constitutional right to vote, including by mail, without interference by USPS,” he wrote.
‘Problems at every stage’
In a final rule published Aug. 21, the Postal Service said states would use a to-be-developed online portal to upload information about the envelopes being used for mail ballots and the voters who received them. USPS would also use the portal to verify that all ballots and voters complied with the requirements set out in the new rule.
But the project was beset with several challenges, in part spurred by the unrealistic timeline for development, the whistleblower said.
The whistleblower’s disclosure “identifies problems at every stage of USPS’s development of the Portal, demonstrating deeply flawed plans for implementation,” Blumenthal wrote.
A project of the portal’s size and importance would normally “take nine months to a year or more” to finish, according to the whistleblower’s disclosure. Smaller current Postal Service IT projects have been given eight-month timelines, according to the whistleblower.
USPS began developing the mail ballot portal in June, just three months before it was to be introduced and less than five months before Election Day, according to the disclosure.
Individual elements of the tool have not been sufficiently tested, “rendering meaningful testing of the project impossible,” the whistleblower said.
“The Whistleblower believes that there has been insufficient internal testing of the system,” the disclosure said. “Such testing is critical to determine whether it will work on September 1, when states could be expected to start using it.”
Software developers on the project have “considerable concern” that the project skipped “standard principles of testing and debugging new software before launch,” the whistleblower said.
One faulty barcode
The IT problems heighten the danger of another major issue: a policy of rejecting entire batches of ballots based on a faulty barcode on a single ballot.
According to the whistleblower, “the administration has hidden the high likelihood” that standard raises for major disruptions in ballot delivery.
“As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state – effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” the report said.
A misread barcode could result from something as simple as a voter’s changed name after marriage or a move of address, Blumenthal said.
Court order
The whistleblower said the USPS paused work for about a month after Judge Indira Talwani in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts issued an injunction against Trump’s executive order, finding, in part, that it likely violated the U.S. Constitution’s provision granting states the power to administer elections.
But USPS officials then ordered work to resume on the project, in defiance of the judicial order that remained in effect, the whistleblower said.
The whistleblower added that the agency ignored another temporary restraining order Talwani, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama, issued last week and upheld Monday, and continued to work on the project.
In his letter to Steiner, Blumenthal asked if that was true and posed several other questions stemming from the whistleblower’s report, and asked for a response by Friday.

USPS, which did not respond to AFP’s request for comment, had been working toward a September 1 launch, the whistleblower said.

“The whistleblower’s allegations make clear that USPS lacks the technical or operational capability needed to effectively implement the [order’s] provisions in a way that safeguards every citizen’s right to vote in the upcoming midterm elections,” Blumenthal said.
“Despite this, the Trump administration appears intent on USPS moving forward with its flawed plans, no matter the chaos they may create.”
Blumenthal told reporters in a press call reported by The New York Times that the USPS had designed the system to “disenfranchise millions”, and noted that about a third of American voters cast ballots by mail.

The Trump administration is appealing.
The judge has, however, allowed USPS to continue work on the online portal for states that choose voluntarily to use it while the wider legal battle continues.
The dispute comes as the first states prepare to send mail ballots this week, leaving election officials with little time to adjust should the courts eventually allow Trump’s rules to take effect.
“Any widespread USPS disruption would cripple election administration in many states, including my home state, Arizona,” said Stephen Richer of the libertarian Cato Institute, a top former administrator for Maricopa County, one of the largest voting jurisdictions in the United States.

We need to get the word out: Do NOT use the USPS to vote in the midterms
This does not mean you can’t vote by mail. My understanding is that states that use vote by mail, either as the standard option as in Colorado and several other states, or as an alternative, whether for absentee voting or just in general, have drop boxes at polling places and elsewhere that allow mailed ballots to be deposited without using the USPS. And that’s a good thing because:
A new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for this November’s US midterm elections was thrown together so hastily, and tested so little, that a single scanning glitch could see entire batches of ballots turned away, a whistleblower has told Congress.
The project – a key part of Donald Trump’s new restrictions on voting – is “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to the US senator Richard Blumenthal, who disclosed the warning in a letter to David Steiner, the postmaster general, on Tuesday.
Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the US Senate’s permanent subcommittee on investigations, said the account he had received made clear the US Postal Service “lacks the technical or operational capability” to roll it out safely before ballots go out to voters.
The system stems from a March executive order by Trump tightening federal control over mail-in voting, directing USPS to check ballots against a federally approved voter list before sending them – a break from its usual role of simply delivering whatever is handed over by states. Courts have blocked and unblocked parts of the order repeatedly since, amid lawsuits arguing it oversteps into territory the constitution leaves to states.
USPS calls the result the “Federal Ballot Mail Portal”. Officials upload voter and barcode data in advance; clerks then scan a sample of arriving ballots – 15 to 400, depending on batch size – against that list. According to the whistleblower’s disclosure, the system runs on a “zero percent failure rate”: one mismatched scan rejects the entire batch, even if it holds tens of thousands of ballots.
This is just PRI-level bullshit, to operationalize the real voter fraud, which is what the Trump administration is going to be engaging in on a massive scale. (As always, IAIAC!).
My large-scale organizational skills are non-existent, but let’s all do what we can to get the word out: DON’T trust the USPS with your vote. If you can’t or don’t want to vote in-person, which at this point huge numbers of people have every legitimate reason not to want to do any more, drop your ballot off personally, rather than turning it over to the Trump administration, which is what mailing it via the US Mail is.
. . . commenters are pointing out that some of the ungovernable tribal regions DON’T have drop boxes, and that part of the fuckery here is to keep people from getting ballots at all, so they can’t return them. Unfortunately a lot of the GOTV effort is apparently going to have to focus on physically getting people to polling places, to vote in person, hopefully early if not often.

sources.text:
A whistleblower has warned Congress that the US Postal Service is moving ahead with a new system to enforce President Donald Trump’s restrictions on mail-in voting, raising concerns that technical errors could lead to legitimate ballots being rejected or delayed.
The allegations have drawn scrutiny from Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, who has asked Postmaster General David Steiner to provide documents and answer questions about the system.
According to the whistleblower’s claims cited by Blumenthal, USPS is preparing a system with what the senator described as an “impracticable zero percent failure rate.”
Under the system, even a single problem matching a ballot to an approved voter could potentially affect an entire batch of ballots.
Blumenthal gave a hypothetical example: If election officials delivered 10,000 ballots and USPS could not match one because the voter had recently changed their name or moved, the other 9,999 ballots could also be refused for delivery.
The concern is that legitimate voters could lose access to their ballots because of administrative or computer-system errors.
Trump signed an executive order in March seeking to impose new restrictions on mail-in voting.
Among other measures, the order directed the Department of Homeland Security to provide states with information on citizens eligible to vote. It also directed the Justice Department to prioritize investigations involving officials accused of issuing ballots to people considered ineligible.
The order further instructed USPS to deliver mail ballots only to voters appearing on each state's approved mail-ballot list.
The administration has described the measures as efforts to strengthen election security and prevent voting by ineligible people.
The Postal Service is responsible for delivering mail-in ballots once they are sent by election officials.
The new system is intended to help USPS check ballot information against voter lists before delivering the ballots.
Critics, however, argue that putting additional verification requirements into the postal system could create new opportunities for legitimate ballots to be rejected.
USPS had not immediately commented on Blumenthal's allegations.
The US Supreme Court last week lifted a lower-court order that had blocked the Trump administration from implementing the executive order. However, a separate injunction covering a key part of the plan remains in effect.
That means the administration has gained some room to proceed, but the broader legal fight over Trump's mail-voting restrictions is not over.
The timing is significant because the 2026 congressional midterm elections are scheduled for November.
Mail voting is widely used in the US, particularly by voters who cannot or do not want to vote in person on Election Day. Any system that delays or rejects legitimate ballots could therefore affect access to voting.
Blumenthal has accused USPS of creating a system that could disenfranchise voters, while Trump has repeatedly argued that mail voting is vulnerable to fraud.
However, documented cases of voter fraud involving mail ballots are rare.

Whistleblower Warns of Chaotic Trump Plan to Meddle With USPS Ballot Processing
sources.text:
Whistleblower Warns of Chaotic Trump Plan to Meddle With USPS Ballot Processing
A whistleblower within the United States Postal Service (USPS) is warning of covert plans by the Trump administration to reshape the nation’s mail-in ballot verification system in ways that could disenfranchise scores of American voters.
According to a letter released by Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) on Tuesday, his office received information about a whistleblower disclosure alleging that the Trump administration intends to give USPS broad authority to refuse to mail electoral ballots. “USPS will, for the first time, play a gatekeeping function and be in a position to refuse to mail ballots that state election officials have determined should be sent out,” the letter says,” and will do so via an error riddled platform that was rush ordered by the administration.
Last month, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to implement mail-in voting restrictions outlined in an executive order signed by the president in March. Among other provisions, the order requires states to provide the USPS with lists of all the voters it intends to issue return-by-mail ballots to, and grants the agency the authority to refuse to mail out the ballot.
The whistleblower contends that, given the manner the order is being implemented, a single discrepancy in the lists provided to USPS could result in batches of thousands of ballots being rejected en masse.
“Not only is this system astonishingly untested, USPS has simultaneously implemented an impracticable zero percent failure rate,” the letter reads, “When ballots are submitted to USPS in large-volume batches, if any one ballot in the batch cannot be verified against the Portal, all ballots in that batch will be rejected.”
The whistleblower wrote in their report that the current expectation is that states would have to take back thousands of ballots to cure a single issue with a registration or the list, leading to delays and other complications for voters. “Should the slapdash Portal mistakenly mark a ballot as unverified, there is no clear process by which state election officials or voters themselves can challenge the rejection,” Blumenthal’s office added.
White House Spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to Rolling Stone that “The process of building software to carry out this new verification check is neither complex nor unique for USPS since the Postal Service regularly uses bulk mailing and intelligent mail barcodes for a wide variety of large customers. Under President Trump, the federal government is working to ensure safe, transparent, and honest elections.”
The White House did not address separate questions posed by Rolling Stone regarding whether USPS would implement a system to notify individuals whose ballots were rejected, or allow them to challenge any discrepancies.
Furthermore, the whistleblower alleges that the program built to process the millions of mail in ballots expected for the November midterms has not been properly tested, and is error prone.
The portal was built in roughly a three month timespan — with a one month pause as the courts litigated the constitutionality of the executive order. “As a result of this rushed process, USPS has been unable to conduct tests of the Portal to ensure its proper functioning, troubleshoot problems, or distribute instructions on use to state election officials,” the letter relays.
Trump, who himself voted by mail for a special election in Florida earlier this year, has said in the past that “mail-in voting means mail-in cheating.” While the GOP has attempted to associate mail and absentee voting with Democratic constituencies, nearly one in five registered Republicans vote by mail. Their plans to restrict the practice for their opposition could just as easily disenfranchise their own voters.
Fraud in American elections takes place at microscopic rates, but Americans should worry about the integrity of their elections, as MAGA Republicans are waging a multi front war against the freedom to vote.

sources.news_title: 'Catastrophic failures': Whistleblower warns Trump-proposed USPS mail-in ballot system could 'derail' midterms
sources.text:
(WASHINGTON) — An anonymous government employee whistleblower has come forward to Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, warning that a “rushed, chaotic and fundamentally flawed” effort by the U.S. Postal Service to implement President Donald Trump’s mail-in ballot executive order risks a “catastrophic failure” of the election system that could “derail the midterm elections.”
The whistleblower’s concerns were made public in a report released by Blumenthal, who said in a release Tuesday morning that the allegations show that the system USPS is creating to track mail-in balloting is “set up to fail — and risk the right to vote for millions of Americans who cast their ballots by mail.”
The whistleblower is described in the report as someone with direct knowledge of potentially “catastrophic problems” in the development of the USPS’ new electronic federal mail ballot portal.
Under the new proposed system, states would be required to report basic voter information, such as a voter’s name and home address, attached to a unique barcode on every mail-in ballot distributed. Postal workers would then only deliver ballots addressed to voters who appear on the state-provided list.
The new USPS system, published formally last week, was temporarily put on hold by a federal judge as she considers whether it is likely unlawful and should be blocked during an ongoing legal battle. It’s unclear what parts, if any, will be allowed to take effect in time for the November election.
The USPS rules fall short of Trump’s expectations in his executive order.
The first mail-in ballots go out to overseas military voters from North Carolina this Friday. Given the length of the legal battle ahead, it’s unlikely Trump’s proposed changes to mail-in voting will be implemented in time for the midterm elections.
Voter advocates and civil liberties groups worry the rules could prevent some legitimate, eligible voters from receiving ballots. They fear an added bureaucratic layer — such as having to submit lists to a federal portal to be administered by USPS — unduly introduces the risk of errors not to mention the potential for federal meddling.
The whistleblower report also alleges that officials may have defied a prior court-ordered pause, continuing work on the USPS system despite a judge’s instructions.
Blumenthal wrote a letter to Postmaster General and CEO David Steiner on Monday demanding further answers to questions related to allegation raised by the whistleblower and to urge him to “abandon this ill-conceived, unconscionable plan and ensure that all Americans can exercise their constitutional right to vote, including by mail, without interference by USPS.”
ABC News reached out to USPS and the White House for comment on Blumenthal’s letter, but did not immediately receive a response.
‘Slapdash’ assembly of new portal could lead to major issues in November
The whistleblower described a “secretive, rushed, chaotic and fundamentally flawed process” creating and implementing an “untested” federal ballot mail portal that USPS will use to screen ballots.
The rushed effort to create the portal could cause “significant operating” problems and the failure to verify ballots this November, the whistleblower said. It could also mean, the report alleges, that “potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner or at all.”
The report details a “slapdash” production process for the new IT software, which the whistleblower alleges hasn’t been sufficiently tested or debugged. At the time of report, the whistleblower said there was insufficient time to test the system before a Sept. 1 deadline to deliver it.
“According to the whistleblower, USPS’s effort to develop and deploy the Portal has been ‘rushed,’ ‘risky and haphazard’ because leadership has demanded a impossible timeframe. In an effort to meet impossible deadlines, USPS has eliminated standard and needed testing, thereby creating substantial risk of a ‘catastrophic failure’ of the system that could ‘derail the midterm elections,'” Blumenthal wrote in his letter to Steiner.
Blumenthal also raised concerns about a new so-called “zero percent failure rate” which, according to the whistleblower, could see whole batches of ballots being rejected if a barcode on even one ballot fails to scan.
“Voters intending to cast ballots by mail may not even be aware that their ballots have been rejected, or were part of a rejected batch, until it is too late to secure an alternative ballot or vote in person,” Blumenthal wrote.
Whistleblower alleges that work on USPS portal potentially violated court orders
The whistleblower also alleges that — after a one-month pause on work that began in June — employees were told to continue working on the mail-in-ballot portal in July despite an active temporary restraining order from a federal judge ordering a pause on work related to Trump’s mail-in-ballot executive order.
“The project was suddenly resumed without explanation of what authority permitted USPS to ignore the court order,” according to the whistleblower report.
The USPS is currently under a 14-day Temporary Restraining Order issued by Judge Indira Talwani prohibiting it from implementing its new rules for mail ballots ahead of the November election. The judge is hearing arguments on Thursday as to whether to extend the TRO to a preliminary injunction during litigation.
The same judge has already accused the administration of flouting a previous order that had blocked any finalization of the rules while she was considering the matter.
“Based on this timeline, USPS should have ceased all work on the Portal on June 25, 2026, with the earliest conceivable date to resume being August 26, 2026. The whistleblower allegations demonstrate that was not the case, with USPS directing work to continue on the Portal after the first court order to cease work and prior to the recent court decisions allowing USPS to proceed,” Blumenthal wrote to Steiner.
For most voters, nothing is likely to change how they cast ballots by mail in the midterm elections. But the longer the court hold remains in place — and the longer the court fight takes — the less likely it is that any of the rules will practically impact November.
Still, the battle over these rules and any additional ones Trump may seek to impose will continue well into 2028, where the effects could most significantly be felt.

Whistleblower Warns Trump-Ordered USPS Barcode Rule's 'Zero Percent Fail Rate' Could Doom Millions of Ballots
Whistleblower reveals potential disenfranchisement risk due to USPS barcode policy
An anonymous whistleblower has warned that a Trump-ordered United States Postal Service barcode rule, which reportedly enforces a 'zero per cent failure' standard, could stop millions of mail-in ballots from being delivered in November's midterm elections.
In a report submitted to Senator Richard Blumenthal this week, the whistleblower claimed that a single scanning error in a batch of election mail could invalidate the entire bundle and force postal workers to return it to local officials.
The Postal Service finalised a new policy based on a 31 March executive order from President Donald Trump, restricting mail-in voting to states complying with strict federal reporting requirements.
Assessing the Impact of the USPS Barcode Rule
The regulation forces local election administrators to submit voter addresses into a newly established federal portal. Only voters cleared through this database will receive ballots in envelopes marked with special federal barcodes.
Whistleblower Aid, the legal group representing the federal official, warned of a foreseeable disruption to nationwide elections, alleging that the administration has concealed the high probability that these verification processes will result in major delivery failures.
The primary issue lies in the strict enforcement mechanism, which voting rights advocates argue adds administrative hurdles. The United States Postal Service is allegedly implementing a 'zero per cent failure policy' for these newly mandated barcodes.
If a postal scanner fails to read even one barcode in a large bundle of election mail, the entire batch is rejected. The whistleblower noted that predictable errors in any scanning process make this standard difficult to meet, creating a bottleneck that could affect the midterms.
Legal Battles Over the Rule's Implementation
The judicial trajectory of this policy has been fractured. Lower courts initially halted the mandate over the summer before the Supreme Court ruled in a 6–3 decision to lift an injunction, noting that the states' initial lawsuits were premature because the rule was only proposed.
However, once the Postal Service officially finalised the rule in late August, Democratic attorneys general immediately updated their legal challenges.
This shift prompted Judge Indira Talwani to issue a fresh 14-day restraining order.
She determined that government arguments were outweighed by the risk of widespread disenfranchisement of citizens who need access to mail-in ballots to vote.
A federal appeals court is currently weighing whether to lift her temporary order. The debate over whether the mandate will be active for the midterms must be resolved urgently, given that some states begin mailing ballots as early as September.
How the USPS Rule Impacts the Electorate
Voters do not need to take extra steps under the new framework, but they bear the ultimate risk of the administrative burden placed on local officials.
The rule demands that election boards design new envelopes, secure federal approval, train staff on the new portal and upload citizen data at least 30 days before the election. In her ruling, Judge Talwani noted that states lack the time and funds to achieve this timeline, raising concerns about subsequent postal delays.
The Postal Service has maintained that the policy is not intended to facilitate voter suppression, claiming it will merely process the data provided without actively verifying voter eligibility.
While Postmaster General David Steiner previously testified to Congress that he would comply with court orders regarding voting by mail, the agency has faced criticism for finalising the 95-page rule despite ongoing legal injunctions.
Voting rights groups argue the logistical reality tells a different story. Disabled voters and senior citizens face heightened risks if batches of mail are returned over a single error.
With early voting deadlines approaching, the primary question is not just whether the courts will strike down the mandate permanently, but how the new administrative requirements might ultimately impact the successful delivery of ballots.

sources.news_title: Sen. Blumenthal Probes New USPS Mail-In Ballot System Amid Whistleblower Complaint
sources.text:
Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) is seeking answers from the postal service about a new platform it is launching that will verify that mail-in ballots are only being sent to eligible voters.
The U.S. Postal Service (USPS) is developing an online portal that allows states to upload a list of eligible voters that the postal system will match against ballots before it mails them out. If a name on a ballot does not appear on the list, USPS will not send out that ballot.
In an Aug. 31 letter to Postmaster General David Steiner and other postal officials, Blumenthal says that process allows USPS to “play a gatekeeping function and be in a position to refuse to mail ballots that state election officials have determined should be sent out.”
“We urge you to abandon this ill-conceived, unconscionable plan and ensure that all Americans can exercise their constitutional right to vote, including by mail, without interference by USPS.”
The senator said he received an anonymous whistleblower complaint alleging the new system is being rushed out in time for the 2026 midterms, but without proper protocols to test whether it functions properly.
The whistleblower said USPS is using a “zero percent failure rate” system: In a batch of 10,000 ballots, if even one ballot doesn’t match the voter list—or if one barcode doesn’t scan properly—the entire batch will be sent back to the state for reverification.
Blumenthal also wants to know whether USPS violated multiple court orders by continuing work on the system.
The mail-in voting changes stem from President Donald Trump’s executive order seeking to regulate the practice for election integrity. The government has an “unavoidable duty” under the Constitution to ensure election laws are enforced, Trump wrote in the March order.
The new portal has been in development since June, but U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani ordered USPS to halt work on it—along with other parts of Trump’s order—in a court order that remained in force for about a month. The Supreme Court struck down Talwani’s order at the end of August. The justices said she acted prematurely, since USPS had not finalized its new mail-in voting rules.
But USPS issued a final plan on Aug. 21, and that allowed plaintiffs to file a fresh lawsuit. Talwani issued another block on Aug. 27, but the whistleblower alleged work on the new system is ongoing despite her order.
Blumenthal is asking USPS to confirm that development of the new system has halted in compliance with Talwani’s order, along with details about who is working on the new system, when the work resumed if that is the case, and what kind of testing USPS plans for the new system before its rollout.
The Epoch Times reached out to the White House and Postmaster General’s office for comment but did not hear back by the time of publication.

Whistleblower says Trump officials are defying court orders on voting by mail
WASHINGTON >> A U.S. Postal Service official has alleged that the agency is moving forward with a “secretive, rushed” effort to implement President Donald Trump’s order exerting federal control over mail voting, despite a court order blocking those plans.
The official filed a whistleblower report, published this morning by the office of Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., asserting that the “risky and haphazard” implementation of Trump’s order could lead to a “catastrophic failure” in the mail ballot system before this year’s midterm elections. The report said the agency had planned to complete the new digital system overseeing mail ballots by today.
“Potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all,” the official said in the report, which was prepared with the assistance of Whistleblower Aid, a nonprofit group that represents people seeking to expose potential lawbreaking.
Speaking to reporters by phone Monday, Blumenthal said of the report that “the main takeaway for me is that the Postal Service has designed a system to disenfranchise millions of Americans. One-third of all Americans cast their ballots by mail, and the USPS puts all of their votes at risk.”
A Postal Service official declined to comment on the record.
Voting by mail will become much more difficult, if not impossible, for tens of millions of Americans if the Postal Service is allowed to implement the restrictive rules governing mail voting that Trump has demanded.

Trump has repeatedly promoted false claims of widespread fraud through mail-in voting, which he has described as “cheating,” “corrupt” and “horrible,” even though he voted by mail in two elections this year. He has moved to restrict mail-in voting using a variety of procedural and legislative levers.
Those moves have led to a pileup of legal rulings and challenges surrounding the nation’s electoral system just two months before the midterm elections. The rules could especially affect states where some of the most competitive races for House, Senate and governor will determine control of Congress and state governments.
Michigan, where 37% of votes were cast by mail in 2022, would be one, with competitive statewide contests and multiple battleground House races. California, which mails ballots to all voters, is expected to be central to Democratic efforts to win control in the House.
The Supreme Court had allowed the Trump administration to move ahead with Trump’s mail ballot executive order, reasoning that a lawsuit challenging the order was premature because the administration had not started implementing its plans.
But days before the court ruled, the Postal Service formally published a new plan to comply with the executive order.
Judge Indira Talwani, a U.S. District Court judge in Massachusetts, reasoned that the stakes had changed with the new plan and temporarily blocked it, concluding that the agency’s plan appeared to overstep its legal mandate and could spark chaos by changing rules a little more than two months before an election.
The whistleblower report provided specific details of the Postal Service’s effort to rapidly implement a new digital system for mail ballots, even as a federal appeals court had blocked the plan before the Supreme Court intervened. Work has also continued on the system even after Talwani ordered the plan halted last week, the report said.
The official at the Postal Service raised “grave concerns” in the report that the verification process in the system could reject tens of thousands of ballots in a bulk-mailing batch if “even one bar code on one single ballot” failed to properly scan, and that the rushed, “slapdash” development of the system would significantly increase the chance of errors and other failures in the verification process.

sources.news_title: USPS whistleblower exposes hidden plan that could disrupt mail-in voting
sources.text:
A whistleblower is raising the alarm over a new U.S. Postal Service system for verifying mail ballots, alleging that the plan has been kept from the public and that the agency is rushing the system into operation ahead of the midterm elections.
The allegations are contained in a new report released Tuesday by Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal. The report was prepared by attorneys representing an unnamed USPS whistleblower.
According to the report, Postal Service employees have privately expressed serious concerns about the system’s development, with multiple people allegedly describing the rollout as a “sh*t show.”
The whistleblower says USPS leadership has pushed ahead despite changing technical requirements, inadequate testing and an extremely compressed development schedule, CNN reports.
“USPS leadership, it appears, has discarded all best practices as they speed the project to be ready for a September 1 implementation,” the report says, raising questions about whether a potentially catastrophic failure could become “a feature rather than a bug.”
At the heart of the controversy is a system created after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March giving USPS an unprecedented role in screening state mail-ballot programs.
Under the plan, states would provide USPS with lists of voters who are expected to receive mail ballots.
The Postal Service would then compare that information with data associated with ballot envelopes.
And according to the whistleblower, the process could be extremely unforgiving.
One mismatch could hold up thousands of ballots.
The report alleges that the system includes verification procedures that aren’t fully spelled out in the publicly available regulations.
In one stage, information uploaded by election officials would reportedly be compared against “manifests” submitted for each batch of ballots.
Those manifests would include information such as unique bar codes assigned to individual voters.
The whistleblower alleges that the information would have to match the data in the USPS system before election officials could proceed with delivering the ballots.
Then comes another verification step.
When election officials bring ballot envelopes to a USPS facility, the envelopes could either be scanned individually or sampled, depending on the location.
According to the whistleblower, if even one ballot envelope fails to match the information in the system, USPS could refuse delivery of the entire batch.
That could potentially put thousands of ballots on hold at once.
“As designed, the process is entirely unforgiving,” the report says. “It could delay ballots by the thousands in repeated verification cycles — and thus prevent states from mailing enormous numbers of ballots.”
The concern is particularly significant because election officials work under strict deadlines. A delay isn’t simply an inconvenience when ballots must reach voters, be returned and processed before election deadlines.
The whistleblower’s concerns go beyond how the system works.
The report also describes what it characterizes as a chaotic development process.
USPS information-technology teams were allegedly given less than a week to test the system once development was completed.
The reason was the rapidly approaching election calendar.
North Carolina was scheduled to begin sending ballots this week, with other states following later in September.
According to the whistleblower, system requirements were “constantly changing” throughout development.
The requirements also allegedly weren’t clearly documented for the employees building the system.
USPS leadership, the report says, dismissed concerns about the lack of written requirements and insisted employees understood what was needed — while simultaneously saying there wasn’t enough time to document everything.
The testing schedule allegedly made matters worse.
Under the timeline for a September 1 implementation, only four days were allotted for a stage in which potential users could test the system.
“For a system that manages something as important as handling voting and ballots, 4 days of user testing is entirely unreasonable,” the whistleblower report says.
Courts are already fighting over the plan
The dispute isn’t happening in a vacuum.
Multiple courts are considering challenges to the administration’s mail-ballot requirements.
A judge last week froze the requirement that states use the USPS system if they want the Postal Service to deliver their ballots.
The ruling nevertheless allowed USPS to make the portal available to states that voluntarily choose to upload mail-voter information.
The Justice Department is appealing the decision.
Meanwhile, the whistleblower report says it remains unclear whether the portal was actually ready for the September 1 target date.
That leaves election officials facing a system that, according to the allegations, has been developed under intense time pressure and subjected to limited testing.
And there’s another unusual element to the controversy.
Some of the procedures described by the whistleblower allegedly aren’t contained in the public regulations governing the system.
That means election officials may have to navigate requirements that weren’t fully visible when the rules were announced.
The stakes are enormous
The Postal Service handles millions of pieces of election mail.
Under the system described in the whistleblower report, however, the problem wouldn’t necessarily have to be widespread to create widespread consequences.
A technical error, data mismatch or scanning problem could potentially prevent an entire batch of ballot envelopes from being delivered until officials identify and correct the discrepancy.
The whistleblower argues that repeated verification cycles could therefore delay large numbers of ballots.
According to the whistleblower, USPS has been racing toward implementation while technical requirements continue to change and testing time remains extremely limited.
With courts still weighing the legality of the requirements and election officials already preparing for mail-ballot deadlines, there is little room for a systemwide technical failure.
And if the whistleblower’s concerns prove justified, the consequences wouldn’t be confined to a broken piece of software.
They could show up in the form of delayed ballots, potentially by the thousands.

With nine weeks before Election Day, a federal whistleblower is raising alarm that the U.S. Postal Service’s rushed implementation of a new and untested system to screen mail ballots, which has been blocked by a federal court, has the potential to upend the upcoming midterm elections.
In a new disclosure made public by Connecticut senator Richard Blumenthal, the unnamed federal official claims that the USPS began work on a new online portal in June with the goal of being operational for a planned September 1 launch date in order to comply with President Donald Trump’s March executive order that introduced new restrictions on mail ballots.
But the whistleblower alleges that the truncated timeline hasn’t allowed for thorough testing of the system, which could result in large swathes of mail-in ballots being rejected or never mailed out to voters at all.
“The apparently sloppy and rushed manner in which the Federal Ballot Mail Portal and supporting IT systems are being built poses significant risk. Potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all. The Whistleblower’s assessment and recitation of the facts around the risky and haphazard development of the project is a compelling warning of catastrophic failure which could derail the midterm elections,” wrote attorneys with
Whistleblower Aid, a legal nonprofit that aids and represents whistleblowers.
The official’s disclosure lays out one particular nightmare scenario involving the new system’s barcode-verification protocol. Per the whistleblower, the agency has adopted a “zero percent failure” policy where if a scanner fails to verify the barcode on a single ballot in a batch submitted to be mailed by state officials, the entire batch will be rejected and sent back to the state in order for the error to be corrected. The submitted batches could contain as many as 10,000 ballots and voters are unlikely to know that their requested ballot has been rejected. “Even under ordinary circumstances this would be problematic because of predictable errors in any barcode scanning process,” the complaint read.
In the lead-up to the Tuesday implementation deadline, the whistleblower said they believed there has been “insufficient internal testing” of the new USPS system even as multiple states are slated to begin using it. In their complaint, the federal official noted that there would be less than a week of testing of the IT systems, adding they were aware of several USPS officials describing the process in the lead-up to the deadline as “a shit show.”

Trump’s executive order, which mandates the creation of state citizenship lists of eligible voters and new mail-ballot designs, has been challenged by state election officials and others who argue the new requirements are too arduous to implement in time for voters to receive their ballots. While work on the new systems was halted by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani’s order in June, it reportedly resumed a month later despite that order. On Thursday, Talwani once again blocked attempts to implement Trump’s executive order just days after the U.S. Supreme Court issued a stay on Talwani’s June order, a ruling that left the door open for further legal challenges and a potential return to the Court.
In a letter accompanying the whistleblower’s disclosure, Blumenthal asked Postmaster General David Steiner questions surrounding the online portal’s implementation and testing, seeking a response by September 8. The senator, who serves on the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, urged the USPS official to drop the agency’s plans.

An anonymous federal official has warned members of Congress that Donald Trump’s “secretive, rushed” and “chaotic” plans for the U.S. Postal Service to implement new rules for mail-in ballots could disenfranchise millions of voters this fall.
Tuesday’s whistleblower report outlines “potentially catastrophic problems” with the administration’s brand-new system, including a “zero-percent failure policy” that could reject tens of thousands of ballots at a time if any single mistakes are made, including misread barcodes or inadvertent errors from postal workers.
Postal officials and IT specialists called it a “mess” and a “s*** show” that illegally defied court orders against putting the new ballot-tracking system in place ahead of crucial midterm elections, according to the report.
“We are crossing the Rubicon of American elections,” said Libby Liu, CEO of WhistleblowerAid.org, which is representing the anonymous official who submitted the complaints.
“This dangerously defective mail-in ballot process could disenfranchise millions of voters, ensnaring ballots in red tape under the guise of solving a non-existent problem,” she added. “People in states that rely heavily on vote-by-mail will have a more difficult time making their voices heard in our challenged democracy this November. The whistleblower’s service to our nation is warning the public that their ability to vote is in serious jeopardy.”
Federal courts have repeatedly blocked the Postal Service from implementing Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots, which called for the creation of a national voter registration list that would be used to decide who is eligible to cast a ballot.
On August 21, the USPS published its new certification requirements, changes that could not go into effect until federal courts lifted an injunction against them. The Supreme Court allowed Trump’s executive order to stand, for now, leaving the door open for lawsuits to proceed against the new USPS rules themselves.
Three days after the Supreme Court’s decision, District Judge Indira Talwani issued a temporary restraining order that blocks the changes, but the administration is continuing to fight the case in court to overhaul mail-in voting rules just weeks before Election Day.
Dozens of election officials from across the country have repeatedly warned that a last-minute scramble to upload lists of voters into an online portal designed by USPS would amount to an unconstitutional attack on election administration that would only sow more confusion and introduce potentially catastrophic errors.
If the plans are allowed to go into effect, USPS workers would be required to scan barcodes on a sample of envelopes to ensure the voters appear on the state’s list, according to the whistleblower report. If there is even one mismatch, that whole batch of ballots — which could be in the thousands at a time — could be rejected, the whistleblower said.
“As designed, the process is entirely unforgiving,” according to the report. “It could delay ballots by the thousands in repeated verification cycles — and thus prevent states from mailing enormous numbers of ballots.”
States are constantly updating their voter rolls, the lists sent to USPS could be out of date shortly after voters re-register with new personal information or addresses, or if new voters sign up but aren’t reflected in the already-approved list designed by the administration.
USPS and the Department of Justice have repeatedly defended the program, though election officials fear the government’s list could be dangerously too slow to reflect changes from the states.
“Their system is set up to fail — and risk the right to vote for millions of Americans who cast their ballots by mail,” according to Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, whose office received the whistleblower report.
“Given this new information, such sloppiness and haste seems clearly part of a purposeful attempt to create chaos and prevent people from voting,” he said in a statement Tuesday. “I am demanding answers and accountability.”
Voting rights groups fear the president’s efforts to centralize control over election administration, which is left to the states under the Constitution, is an attempt to boost Republican candidates and suppress Democratic turnout during an election that is likely to determine the balance of power in Congress — and the fate of Trump’s remaining years in office.
Trump spent years baselessly insisting that voting by mail is ripe for fraud, and that manipulated ballots were “rigged” against him in elections he lost. He complained throughout 2020 elections that Republicans would “never” win without changing rules for voting by mail, which he has called “inherently corrupt” and “cheating” despite routinely casting his own ballots by mail.
The administration is pushing for mail-in ballot changes in court while the president simultaneously demands Senate passage his SAVE America Act, which would also severely restrict mail-in voting and impose nationwide voter ID rules, among other changes.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune has repeatedly expressed doubts about sacrificing the filibuster to pass Trump’s bill. Still, Trump has tried to argue for its passage in increasingly desperate terms, including not ruling out the possibility of a national emergency to put the rules in place.
“The crown jewel of American democracy, our historic record of free and fair elections, deserves so much better than this slipshod effort,” WhistleblowerAid.org senior vice president and special counsel David Kligerman, who is representing the whistleblower, said in a statement.
States are scrambling to prepare for midterm elections, with impending deadlines for voters to receive ballots that can be filled out and returned in time to count by November.
Officials in North Carolina have already started preparing ballots under a new state law requiring voters to start receiving them 60 days before an election. More states are set to start mailing out ballots in the coming days and weeks.
But the “slapdash rollout” of Trump’s new system “could prove a major threat to voting rights in upcoming midterm elections,” Kligerman said. “We hope that the courts across the country looking at this issue are able to take note of these fundamentally troubling revelations.”
Members of the House Oversight Committee are also sounding alarms.
Rep. Robert Garcia, the committee’s top Democrat, joined all Democrats on the committee in a letter to the Postmaster General, warning that the administration’s“reckless actions undermine the foundation of our nation’s democracy and violate the basic principle that all citizens have the right to have their vote counted.”
“We demand that you immediately cease implementation of this irresponsible and illegal scheme to implement the Trump Administration’s plan to control our federal elections,” they wrote.
In a statement, Garcia blasted the USPS measure as a “power grab.”
“The Trump administration’s illegal effort to interfere with our elections must be stopped immediately and we are fighting this attack on our voting system in the courts,” he said.

Whistleblower says USPS defied court to push ‘untested’ portal for Trump mail voting order
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A Postal Service whistleblower says a rushed, error-filled computer system tied to President Trump’s new mail voting order could delay or block ballots for millions of Americans this fall.
- Trump’s March order requires USPS to send ballots only to voters on new federal citizenship lists, and is currently being fought by California and other states, voting rights groups and Democratic organizations in court.
The U.S. Postal Service is rushing to implement President Trump’s new rules for mail ballots — despite a court order barring it from doing so — using “an entirely new and untested set of IT systems” that could cause “catastrophic problems” in the November election, according to an agency whistleblower.
“Potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all,” the unidentified whistleblower alleged in a statement published Tuesday by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), the ranking Democrat on the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.
Among other issues, the whistleblower alleged that the Postal Service’s new Federal Ballot Mail Portal for verifying mail ballots — which Trump demanded in a March executive order and California and other states are challenging in court — has been built in a “slapdash” manner and is “fundamentally flawed.” Thousands of ballots would be invalidated whenever a single ballot’s newly designed Postal Service barcode isn’t properly read, the whistleblower said.
“As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state — effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” read the whistleblower’s statement, which the group Whistleblower Aid helped draft.
The Postal Service did not respond to a request for comment, but Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, downplayed the concerns.
“The process of building software to carry out this new verification check is neither complex nor unique for USPS since the Postal Service regularly uses bulk mailing and intelligent mail bar codes for a wide variety of large customers,” Bis said. “Under President Trump, the federal government is working to ensure safe, transparent, and honest elections.”
 This new secret tracking system at the U.S. Postal Service is faulty, untested, and threatens to totally disrupt ballot delivery for millions of American citizens
— Rep. Robert Garcia
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, whose office has been leading the state challenge to the Postal Service changes in court, said his office has been “arguing in court that USPS cannot credibly implement the drastic, unprecedented, and unlawful changes at issue in time for the November midterm elections.”
The whistleblower’s statement, he added, “only strengthens that position and underscores the importance of our litigation and other legal challenges to the Trump Administration’s actions.”
Other California leaders expressed outrage and demanded the Postal Service plans be abandoned.
“This new secret tracking system at the U.S. Postal Service is faulty, untested, and threatens to totally disrupt ballot delivery for millions of American citizens,” said Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Long Beach), ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, who said his committee had also received the whistleblower’s statement.
“Defying court orders to engage in election interference should bring prison time. Lock them up. Defend democracy,” Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote on X.
“Our elections are safe and secure. They WORK,” Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) wrote on the same platform. “Trump is trying to sow chaos for mail voting in the midterm elections because prices are up, his policies are unpopular, and he knows the American people are going to be heard loud and clear on Election Day.”
California law requires all registered voters be sent a ballot in the mail, and more than 80% of California voters have used those ballots to vote in recent elections. A majority of state voters in a recent poll identified potential interference in the election by the Trump administration as a “major concern.”
Trump — who votes by mail himself — has contended without evidence that the changes are necessary to combat widespread voter fraud, including by noncitizens. Independent elections experts say there is no evidence that such fraud exists in large numbers.
President Trump has spent months waging an unusually aggressive campaign to reshape how states run elections.
Trump’s executive order called on the Postal Service to change its rules to require each state to submit a list of eligible voters to the Postal Service, and to use new ballot envelopes with digital bar codes allowing the Postal Service to identify and reject any that don’t match the lists.
The order also called on the Department of Homeland Security to develop its own lists of eligible citizen voters by state, ostensibly to be compared against the state lists. The Postal Service’s final rule adopting the changes did not claim authority to dictate which voters may appear on state lists, but said the lists would put federal law enforcement in “a better position to identify any potential issues” with ballots.
 Under President Trump, the federal government is working to ensure safe, transparent, and honest elections
— Lauren Bis, White House spokesperson
Multiple lower court orders in recent months have barred the Postal Service from implementing the changes, though the whistleblower alleged those orders were ignored.
Some of those orders were lifted after the Supreme Court last month found that federal agencies could continue to prepare for the changes prior to implementing them. However, after the Postal Service issued its “final rule” for implementing the changes on Aug. 21, California and other litigants sued again last week — winning another temporary restraining order barring the work.
U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote that the court did not have “any evidence regarding fraudulent absentee or mail-in voting” before it, and that the Postal Service’s “interest in correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement of citizens who need access to mail ballots in order to vote.”
Talwani, who also issued some of the previous orders blocking the changes, has repeatedly expressed concern about the short timeline until the Nov. 3 elections and the Postal Service’s ability to implement the changes in time.
The whistleblower’s statement bolsters such concerns.
The whistleblower described “a slapdash software development process as the USPS attempted to create this complex IT system, with multiple points of ballot review, in a matter of weeks.” The effort, the whistleblower wrote, “deviates dangerously from even the most basic software development best practices.”
The whistleblower noted “significant concern, among those whose job it is to build this software, that the project violates standard principles of testing and debugging new software” before a Tuesday deadline for making the system ready for use by the states, and that “multiple USPS officials” have referred to the development process as a “s— show.”
The whistleblower also said that Postal Service leaders ordered employees to resume work on the system about a month ago, while it was barred by the court.
In a letter to Postmaster General David Steiner, Blumenthal said the whistleblower’s allegations “make clear that USPS lacks the technical or operational capability needed to effectively implement” Trump’s desired changes, and should abandon the effort.
Justin Levitt, a Loyola Law School professor who studies elections and was a senior policy advisor on democracy and voting rights in the Biden White House, said he is not surprised that a nationwide voting system developed in a matter of weeks is “not ready for prime time.”
“This is what happens when you take people who don’t know what they’re doing, and you instruct them to rush to finish a federal IT project without any of the guardrails around what any of this is supposed to look like,” he said.
He also said if the Postal Service continued to build the portal after a court ordered it to stop, that would be a major problem. “When a court says pencils down, that’s supposed to mean pencils down.”
However, Levitt said said he does not think the courts — including the Supreme Court — will actually allow the changes to take effect for November, if ever.
“I don’t see five justices wanting to unleash this level of chaos in the coming elections,” he said.

Whistleblower says USPS deploying new, ‘untested’ IT systems governing mail-in ballots
A newly released whistleblower complaint reveals details about the “rushed” effort by the Trump administration and U.S. Postal Service to install three new restrictive IT systems that would potentially deny thousands of mail-in ballots, if the federal government disagrees on their eligibility.
According to the complaint, written by attorneys at the nonprofit Whistleblower Aid and released by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the individual is a federal employee with “direct knowledge of potentially catastrophic problems” related to USPS’ handling of mail-in ballots for the upcoming 2026 midterm elections.
The person claims that USPS is deploying entirely “new and untested” IT systems, including a new Federal Ballot Mail Portal that would potentially give USPS more control over whether and when voters receive federal mail ballots.
The disclosure describes the portal and other systems as “new IT systems and corresponding protocols [that] will govern the delivery of ballots to voters as soon as the 2026 mid-term federal elections and beyond.” It calls the development process “secretive, rushed, chaotic and fundamentally flawed,” and part of a larger effort by agency leaders to rush implementation of the system ahead of the 2026 elections.
That rush has forced USPS to forgo much of the pre-release testing of those systems to ensure they work as intended and can safely interoperate with other federal systems. As a result, the whistleblower says the portal is so restrictive it can potentially reject large batches of mail-in ballots based on a single identified ballot error.
According to the letter, there are three primary new IT systems USPS is rolling out this election cycle. The Federal Ballot Mail Portal stores both voter names and newly placed ballot barcodes, while a new verification system will compare ballot batch manifests with information in the portal. A third system is described as a new physical barcode sampling verification standard “with a zero percent failure rate.”
“The Whistleblower paints a dire picture of a slapdash software development process as the USPS attempted to create this complex IT system, with multiple points of ballot review, in a matter of weeks,” the letter said. “The very manner in which the project is being developed deviates dangerously from even the most basic software development best practices.”
In all three cases, the onus is explicitly placed on state election officials to resolve discrepancies between federal and state systems.
For example, when the federal government and election officials have different data on batch manifests, which can include tens of thousands of ballots, “election officials will be responsible for resolving any errors purportedly identified in the scan, and for resubmitting the batch manifest – USPS will refuse to accept the ballot batch until the errors are resolved.”
A similarly restrictive approach is described for verifying ballot bar codes.
“As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state – effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” the letter stated.
But the whistleblower said those kinds of small errors are likely to happen in any process that relies on scanning barcodes. In this case, the rushed development and specific location of the barcodes on federal mail ballots means the portal “will almost certainly have significant operating problems.”
The letter says the whistleblower is aware of concerns “among those whose job it is to build this software” that the project is not subject to standard testing and debugging work, and that the systems were escalated to other testing environments before they were even finished. It also claims that the systems’ development was siloed across different teams, with no time to test different software components individually or the system as a whole.
The whistleblower also claims that the USPS rule changes, which have been subject to multiple court injunctions, have continued throughout, in violation of federal court orders. Despite those orders, the agency is believed to have started work on the IT systems in June 2026.
In response, Democrats on the House Committee on Oversight and Reform led by Robert Garcia, D-Calif., wrote to Postmaster General David Steiner saying the disclosures indicate the new IT systems are “faulty” and demanding USPS “immediately cease implementation of this irresponsible and illegal scheme.”
“To be clear, any actions taken by the Postal Service that prevent any registered voter, let alone millions, from voting are unacceptable, a violation of Americans’ voting rights, and likely illegal,” the members wrote.
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said the disclosures could potentially lead to new lawsuits against USPS and the federal government.
“This seems to confirm that the USPS is totally unprepared and unqualified to take on this vast responsibility interjecting itself into state’s mail voting processes,” said Becker on Bluesky. “And could incur liability if USPS truly plans to reject thousands of ballots if there’s even one error.”

sources.text:
Whistleblower warns Trump mail ballot plan could be 'catastrophic'
The whistleblower described a “secretive, rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed process” by the Postal Service to implement the mail ballot plan.
A whistleblower is warning that the technology developed by the U.S. Postal Service to carry out President Donald Trump’s order exerting federal control of mail ballots could "derail the midterm elections," saying it hasn't been properly tested and risks "catastrophic failure" if implemented.
The whistleblower, a federal official with direct knowledge of the plan, describes a “secretive, rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed process" that advanced despite court orders blocking the Postal Service from enacting the mail ballot changes.
“The Whistleblower also raises grave concerns that the administration has hidden the high likelihood that the new ballot mail verification processes will result in major disruptions in mail ballots ever getting delivered to voters,” according to the report, which was prepared by the group Whistleblower Aid and sent to Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Connecticut.
The Postal Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump issued an executive order in March directing the Department of Homeland Security to develop lists of eligible voters in each state and requiring the U.S. Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on the approved lists. The president often has made unfounded claims about widespread problems with mail voting, despite casting his own ballot by mail.
Trump's order escalated his bid to place new restrictions on voting ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, when control of Congress is at stake. It was condemned by Democrats and voting rights groups, who said it interferes with state election administration and makes it harder for people to vote, and quickly challenged in court.

“Just a few weeks later, on or around July 29, 2026, the project was suddenly resumed without explanation of what authority permitted USPS to ignore the court order,” the complaint says in noting the June 25 block.

“Potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all,” the complaint states, while “warning of catastrophic failure which could derail the midterm elections.”
Blumenthal said in a letter to the Postal Service that the agency should scrap the effort.
"We urge you to abandon this ill-conceived, unconscionable plan and ensure that all Americans can exercise their constitutional right to vote, including by mail, without interference," he wrote.
